setupSteps: Choose the support. A solid chair with four legs on a non-slip floor, with a flat, firm seat edge you can grip. Do not use a chair with wheels, a folding chair that can close, a plastic garden chair that flexes, a stool or a sofa that slides. Push on it hard from the side before you start; it must not move. The weight rating of home chairs: Not found; use a gym bench or a heavy dining chair if body weight is high.
Block the chair. Push the chair against a wall (back to the wall) or place a rubber mat under its legs so it cannot slide backwards.

Hand position. Sit on the front edge. Put your palms on the seat edge beside your hips (not far behind), shoulder-width apart or a hand-width inside, fingers pointing forward and gripping the edge, thumbs wrapped round it.

Slide off. Walk the feet forward and slide your hips just forward off the seat so your weight is on your hands and your bottom is about 10-15 cm (est.) in front of the edge. Keep the hips close to the chair; the further forward the hips drift, the more the arms are pushed behind the body.

Feet and knees. Beginner: knees bent about 90 degrees (est.), feet flat, under or just in front of the knees. Intermediate: legs straight, heels on the floor. Advanced: heels on a second chair at the same height.
Shoulders. Press down to straighten the arms, then pull the shoulders down and slightly back (away from the ears) and keep the chest open.
Camera. Place the phone at about elbow height, 2 m (est.) to your side, in landscape, so ear, shoulder, elbow, wrist, hip and knee are visible.
Clothing: a fitted short-sleeved or sleeveless top and fitted track pants so the camera can see elbows, hips and knees.
Before the first set: do 30-60 s of shoulder circles and wall push-backs (section 8) as a warm-up, and read section 9 if you have any shoulder, blood pressure or other condition.

steps.part: A. Beginner bent-knee bench dip, partial depth (elbow bend about 100-110 degrees at the bottom)
steps.title: Sit on the chair edge
steps.action: Sit tall on the front edge of the chair, feet flat, knees bent, hands beside your hips.
steps.feel: Even weight through feet and hands; shoulders relaxed.
steps.visualCheck: Side: ear, shoulder and hip in a line, hands under the shoulders' line or just behind it. Front: shoulders level, hands even.

steps.part: A. Beginner bent-knee bench dip, partial depth (elbow bend about 100-110 degrees at the bottom)
steps.title: Grip the edge
steps.action: Grip the seat edge with fingers forward, thumbs round.
steps.feel: Firm, flat palms; no wrist strain.
steps.visualCheck: Front: wrists straight, fingers pointing forward.

steps.part: A. Beginner bent-knee bench dip, partial depth (elbow bend about 100-110 degrees at the bottom)
steps.title: Lift your bottom off the seat
steps.action: Press through the hands and slide your hips forward and off the seat, arms straight, shoulders pulled down.
steps.feel: Weight through the hands and feet, mild work in the arms; elbows not locked hard.
steps.breathing: Breathe out as you press up.
steps.visualCheck: Side: hips about 10-15 cm in front of the seat edge, back upright and close to the chair. Elbow angle about 165-175 degrees (est.).

steps.part: A. Beginner bent-knee bench dip, partial depth (elbow bend about 100-110 degrees at the bottom)
steps.title: Bend the elbows to lower
steps.action: Bend the elbows so the elbows travel straight back and your body goes straight down, close to the chair. Stop when the elbows reach about a 100-110 degree bend (about a hand's width of drop, 10-15 cm, est.). Do not go deeper.
steps.feel: Front of the arms and back of the arms working; no pinch or pain at the front of the shoulder.
steps.visualCheck: Side: back stays close to the chair, shoulders stay down and not touching the ears, upper arm not far behind the trunk. Front: elbows point straight back, not flaring out.

steps.part: A. Beginner bent-knee bench dip, partial depth (elbow bend about 100-110 degrees at the bottom)
steps.title: Pause briefly
steps.action: Pause for 1 second at the shallow bottom, shoulders still pulled down.
steps.feel: Steady; no sinking into the shoulders.
steps.breathing: Brief pause in the breath; do not hold it.
steps.visualCheck: Side: depth does not change between reps.

steps.part: A. Beginner bent-knee bench dip, partial depth (elbow bend about 100-110 degrees at the bottom)
steps.title: Press back up
steps.action: Push through the palms and straighten the elbows until the arms are straight but not locked.
steps.feel: Back of the arms doing the work; chest open.
steps.visualCheck: Side: elbow angle returns to about 160 degrees or more (est.); hips stay close to the chair.

steps.part: A. Beginner bent-knee bench dip, partial depth (elbow bend about 100-110 degrees at the bottom)
steps.title: Repeat
steps.action: Repeat from step 4 with the same depth.
steps.feel: Smooth rhythm; stop if the arms shake or the front shoulder aches.
steps.visualCheck: Same depth and posture on the last rep as the first.

steps.part: A. Beginner bent-knee bench dip, partial depth (elbow bend about 100-110 degrees at the bottom)
steps.title: Finish and rest
steps.action: Press to the top, then sit back on the chair, shake out the arms.
steps.visualCheck: Stop for the day if the front of the shoulder, the wrist or the elbow hurts.

steps.title: Same setup but straighten the legs, heels on the floor, toes up (est.)
Lower to an elbow bend of about 90-100 degrees (est.) and press up. Never deeper than about 90 degrees

Put the heels on a second chair at similar height; hands on the first chair beside the hips. Lower to no deeper than about 90 degrees elbow bend, only if every straight-leg set is pain-free and clean. Chairs must be blocked and stable on a non-slip floor

steps.part: D. Easier options (push-back family, no dip position)
steps.title: Wall push-back: stand an arm's length from a wall, hands on the wall at shoulder height, fingers up. Bend the elbows so your chest nears the wall (elbows close to the body, pointing back), then straighten. 2 s down, 1 s up

steps.part: D. Easier options (push-back family, no dip position)
steps.title: Counter push-back (incline): hands on the edge of a firm kitchen counter or sturdy table, feet back, body straight like a plank leaning in, close-grip, elbows tucked. Lower the chest toward the counter edge and press back. The lower the surface, the harder it gets. This links to the incline push-up in Home 2

steps.part: D. Easier options (push-back family, no dip position)
steps.title: Neither version puts the arm behind the body, so the front-of-shoulder strain is much lower (inference from the shoulder-extension data in section 5, est.)

commonMistakes.title: Going too deep
commonMistakes.text: Going too deep. Why: past about a 90 degree elbow bend the shoulder is pushed far into backward extension, which loads the front of the shoulder joint capsule and structures (the 2022 study authors link this to possible anterior instability over time; this is a theoretical inference, not a measured injury rate; one coaching source argues full-depth controlled dips are not harmful, so sources disagree). Fix: stop at the beginner depth, never below 90 degrees; stop at any front-shoulder pinch.

commonMistakes.title: Hips drifting away from the chair
commonMistakes.text: Hips drifting away from the chair. Why: the arms end up far behind the body and the shoulder extends more. Fix: keep the back close to the chair edge; hips 10-15 cm in front of the seat only.

commonMistakes.title: Shoulders shrugging toward the ears
commonMistakes.text: Shoulders shrugging toward the ears. Why: the upper traps take over when the triceps tire, and the shoulder joint is pinched (coaching sources). Fix: press the shoulders down; stop the set when you cannot.

commonMistakes.title: Elbows flaring out
commonMistakes.text: Elbows flaring out. Why: wider elbows are linked in coaching sources to more front-shoulder stress; I could not verify the study cited for that. Fix: point the elbows straight back.

commonMistakes.title: Using the legs to push up
commonMistakes.text: Using the legs to push up. Why: the legs take over so the triceps work less. Fix: bring the feet closer, or lift only with the arms; use the push-back instead.

commonMistakes.title: Holding the breath
commonMistakes.text: Holding the breath. Why: breath-holding raises blood pressure more than open breathing during effort (lab data from heavy lifting, PubMed 7741618). Fix: breathe in on the way down, out on the way up.

commonMistakes.title: Using an unstable chair
commonMistakes.text: Using an unstable chair. Why: a chair that slides or folds can drop you backwards. Fix: wall behind the chair, mat beneath, test it, use a sturdy chair or bench.

commonMistakes.title: Locking the elbows hard at the top or bouncing at the bottom
commonMistakes.text: Locking the elbows hard at the top or bouncing at the bottom. Why: it jolts the elbow and shoulder joints. Fix: stop just short of locked and lower with a 2 s count.

commonMistakes.title: Hands too far behind or fingers turned inward
commonMistakes.text: Hands too far behind or fingers turned inward. Why: it increases wrist strain and shoulder extension. Fix: hands beside the hips, fingers forward.

commonMistakes.title: Pushing through pain
commonMistakes.text: Pushing through pain. Why: sharp front-shoulder, wrist or elbow pain is a stop sign. Fix: stop, rest, and switch to wall or counter push-backs.

safetyNotes: Shoulder problems (past dislocation, instability, impingement, rotator cuff injury, recent injury or surgery, or a front-shoulder pinch in any overhead or behind-the-back movement): avoid the dip position. Healthline says dips may not be a good choice with an existing shoulder injury and that poor form can cause impingement; ACE and the 2022 study both raise concern for the front of the shoulder. Use wall or counter push-backs, close-grip incline push-ups, or ask a clinician.
Hands behind the body is the risk position. Keep the hands beside the hips, hips close to the chair, and elbow bend never below about 90 degrees; beginners stay around 100-110 degrees (est.).

High blood pressure and heart disease: keep reps low (5-8), moderate effort, no holding the breath, and rise slowly; ask a clinician first if blood pressure is uncontrolled or you have heart disease. A Cooper Institute summary of Sorace et al. suggests beginning upper-body resistance at 30-40% of one-rep maximum and avoiding maximal efforts, which a dip with full body weight cannot be scaled to; so the push-back is the better start (snippet only).
Wrist, elbow or hand pain, or carpal tunnel symptoms: the wrists carry body weight bent back; use the push-back or a fist or neutral-wrist grip only with advice.
Knee, lower back and balance problems: the bent-knee version loads the knees little; keep the back close to the chair; do not use an unstable chair.
Body weight and the chair: high body weight raises the load on the arms and the chair. Use a sturdy chair or gym bench; the weight rating of home chairs: Not found.
Pregnancy, postpartum, recent surgery: ask your clinician before dips.
